AI Predicts Thousands of Mitochondrial Protein Interactions Linked to Human Diseases

Texas A&M AgriLife Research scientists have leveraged an artificial intelligence tool to help answer a long-standing question in human biology regarding what hundreds of mystery proteins inside mitochondria actually do. In a peer-reviewed study titled “The predicted interactome of the human mitochondrial proteome,” published in Nature Communications, the research team computationally screened every possible pairing among approximately 1,100 human mitochondrial proteins—encompassing more than 630,000 combinations—to identify likely interactions. The resulting predictions linked numerous disease-associated proteins to previously unknown biological pathways, pointing researchers toward potential diagnostic and therapeutic targets across a wide spectrum of human illnesses.

Mitochondria serve as the energy centers of human cells, and while scientists have known for years that roughly 1,100 proteins reside within these cellular organelles, the specific functions of many of these molecules have remained uncharacterized. This knowledge gap presents a major biomedical problem because genetic mutations in nearly 30 percent of mitochondrial proteins have been directly linked to human diseases. These medical conditions range from relatively common disorders such as cancer, Parkinson’s disease, and Alzheimer’s disease to rare inherited metabolic disorders. Without understanding the exact biochemical duties of these proteins, scientists face substantial obstacles in establishing the fundamental mechanisms of associated diseases and designing effective treatments.

Because direct biochemical roles can be difficult to measure in isolation, researchers frequently seek to infer a protein’s function by determining which other cellular proteins it binds with or physically contacts. However, traditional laboratory methods for identifying protein interactions are notoriously slow, creating a severe bottleneck for researchers nationwide who are working to understand these mystery proteins. As study lead author Abhinav Swaminathan, Ph.D., an AgriLife Research scientist in the laboratory of Vishal Gohil, Ph.D., professor and Chancellor EDGES Fellow in the Texas A&M Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics, explained, failing to identify the function of individual proteins prevents biomedical researchers from determining how to treat the diseases they may cause.

To overcome the limitations of slow experimental methods, Swaminathan and Gohil set out nearly three years ago to accelerate their investigations by testing an artificial intelligence platform called AlphaFold-Multimer, or AFM. Google DeepMind created and unveiled AlphaFold-Multimer in 2022 to predict the three-dimensional shapes and structural complexes that proteins form together. Swaminathan noted that their laboratory initially lacked reliable experimental tools to directly evaluate mitochondrial protein interactions for the mitochondrial copper pathway proteins they routinely study. After a preliminary trial using the AI approach proved highly successful, the researchers decided to scale the methodology across all human mitochondrial proteins.

Systematically applying the AI tool to screen 630,003 possible pairwise combinations among the approximately 1,100 mitochondrial proteins allowed the team to catalog 2,895 likely interactions. Notably, more than half of these predicted pairings had never been reported in prior scientific literature. Beyond mapping known disease proteins into previously unrecognized cellular pathways, the computational screen achieved a significant basic science milestone by assigning the very first probable interacting partners to 85 previously uncharacterized proteins, providing concrete clues regarding what these mystery molecules do inside living cells.

Following the computational screening phase, the researchers spent approximately two years conducting laboratory experiments to rigorously validate the predicted partnerships in biological model systems. These experimental tests, which included collaborative work carried out with researchers at Washington University School of Medicine in St. Louis, successfully confirmed several of the computational pairings in yeast and human cells. The results demonstrated that AI predictions can serve as an effective road map for laboratory scientists, pinpointing which physical interactions are most likely to yield productive results when subjected to traditional bench testing.

To ensure that the global scientific community can utilize these findings, the team established MitoMatch, a free online resource that allows researchers worldwide to identify and assign likely interacting partners to the specific mitochondrial proteins they study. The comprehensive project was supported by the National Institutes of Health, Texas A&M High Performance Research Computing, and The Welch Foundation. As team members continue experimenting with the data and collaborating with other scientists to understand cell function, Swaminathan noted that while actual cures for mitochondria-linked diseases may remain far in the future, the success of their AI-guided strategy offers a promising starting point for discovery.

Swaminathan reflected on the interdisciplinary approach, emphasizing that their group operates as a traditional biochemistry and genetics laboratory rather than an artificial intelligence laboratory. He explained that the project succeeded because the researchers asked a broader question regarding how to tackle the persistent problem of unknown protein function, using available computational resources creatively to generate an accessible solution for the wider scientific community. By combining predictive structural modeling with wet-lab experimental confirmation, the investigation establishes a systematic framework for uncovering the hidden molecular targets of mitochondrial disease.

Subject of Research: Mitochondrial protein interactome prediction using artificial intelligence

Article Title: Artificial intelligence points researchers toward new disease targets hidden in mitochondria
